patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 5/5] x86/paravirt: Trace contended_release on unlock
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the unlock path for PARAVIRT_SPINLOCKS=y kernels by swapping the target of a static call to a traced unlock function when the contended_release tracepoint is enabled. This reduces overhead when tracing is disabled, as it avoids a branch that would otherwise be taken even if tracing is off. The patch also introduces two new traced unlock functions and updates the pv_is_native_spin_unlock() function accordingly.

review_comments.author: tip-bot2 Ilvokhin
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that the traced unlock variants, native_queued_spin_unlock_traced() and pv_queued_spin_unlock_traced(), do not properly handle the case where the contended_release tracepoint is disabled, leading to a potential lock ordering violation.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 4/5] tracing/lock: Use TRACE_EVENT_FN() for contended_release
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series converts the contended_release trace event to use TRACE_EVENT_FN(), which allows for more flexible and efficient tracing of lock contention. The change involves replacing the static branch that gates the contended_release call with a callback-based approach, using weak no-op hooks for architectures that don't override them.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 3/5] locking/qspinlock: Add contended_release tracepoint
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adds a new tracepoint called contended_release to the qspinlock locking mechanism. The purpose of this tracepoint is to capture information about the holder of a contended spinlock, which is not possible with mutex and rw_semaphore due to their lack of an owner field. The patch combines the contention check, trace call, and release into a single out-of-line function to minimize performance overhead. The patch also introduces a new configuration option to enable or disable this feature, and it includes measurements showing that the binary size impact is minimal even when the tracepoint is enabled.

review_comments.author: tip-bot2 Ilvokhin
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that the patch introduces a performance overhead on some architectures, specifically mentioning x86 and arm64, due to the out-of-line CALL/JMP instructions added for the tracepoint. They also mentioned that the binary size impact is significant (+680 bytes on x86_64), but did not provide any specific concerns about the functionality or correctness of the patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
The following commit has been merged into the locking/core branch of tip:

Commit-ID:     f7e2cb6d495aa1a88368650970a230b45870859b
Gitweb:        https://git.kernel.org/tip/f7e2cb6d495aa1a88368650970a230b45870859b
Author:        Dmitry Ilvokhin <d@ilvokhin.com>
AuthorDate:    Tue, 04 Aug 2026 07:15:43 
Committer:     Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
CommitterDate: Fri, 07 Aug 2026 17:58:10 +02:00

locking/qspinlock: Add contended_release tracepoint

Unlike mutex and rw_semaphore, qspinlock has no owner field, so "perf
lock contention --lock-owner" cannot attribute a contended spinlock to
its holder. The waiter-side contention_begin event records that a
spinlock is contended, but not by whom. Firing contended_release in the
holder's context at unlock is the only way to capture the holder of a
contended spinlock.

Combine the contention check, trace call and release in an out-of-line
queued_spin_release_traced() so the compiler need not preserve the lock
pointer in a callee-saved register across the call.

The check in queued_spin_unlock() is paid on every unlock, even while
the tracepoint is disabled: a static-branch NOP on x86_64, and a few
more instructions to manage a stack frame elsewhere. Gate it behind
CONFIG_QUEUED_SPINLOCKS_TRACE_CONTENDED_RELEASE (default n) so nobody
pays for a tracepoint they do not use. Sleeping locks fire
contended_release regardless.

On x86 this generic path is used only with PARAVIRT_SPINLOCKS=n (e.g.
defconfig). PARAVIRT_SPINLOCKS=y kernels keep the paravirt static_call
unlock and are wired up separately.

All below are with the QUEUED_SPINLOCKS_TRACE_CONTENDED_RELEASE option
enabled.

_raw_spin_unlock(), x86_64 defconfig, GCC 11, tracepoint compiled in but
disabled. The unlock is the single 'movb'. The only instruction added to
the executed path is the 2-byte static-branch NOP. The CALL to the
traced helper and the JMP back are emitted out of line and are reached
only once the static branch is patched on:

          endbr64                            ; 4 bytes
          xchg   %ax,%ax                     ; 2 static-branch NOP
                                             ;   (added)
          movb   $0x0,(%rdi)                 ; 3 unlock (single store)
       A: decl   %gs:__preempt_count         ; 7
          je     B                           ; 2
          jmp    __x86_return_thunk          ; 5
          call   queued_spin_release_traced  ; 5 out of line, reached
                                             ;   only when the
                                             ;   tracepoint is on
          jmp    A                           ; 2 (added)
       B: call   __SCT__preempt_schedule     ; 5
          jmp    __x86_return_thunk          ; 5

Baseline is the same stream without the NOP and the out-of-line
CALL/JMP: 31 bytes vs 40 (+9 bytes).

Binary size impact on x86_64, defconfig: +680 bytes (+0.00%), since all
standard configs out-of-line unlock. Architectures with inlined unlock
(s390 (always), csky and loongarch (both when !PREEMPTION)) will see a
bigger increase in binary size.

On the same path (x86_64, PARAVIRT_SPINLOCKS=n) with the tracepoint
disabled, a _raw_spin_unlock()-heavy nginx workload [1] shows no
measurable difference between baseline and patched kernels in
throughput, latency, cycles, instructions, IPC, or L1 instruction-cache
misses (kernel and total): all deltas stay within run-to-run noise.

Unlike x86, on arm64 the frame setup code (STP, MOV and LDP) lands on
the executed path in addition to static-branch NOP. Binary size impact
on arm64, defconfig: +932 bytes (+0.00%).

The _raw_spin_unlock()-heavy nginx workload reflects the larger hot
path: L1 instruction-cache misses rise ~1.4% (kernel and total) and
instruction count ~0.4%, consistent with the per-unlock frame.
cpu_cycles, throughput and latency show no measurable change and are
within run-to-run noise.

Architectures with fully custom qspinlock implementations (e.g.
PowerPC) are not covered by this change.

[1]: https://lore.kernel.org/all/aiphFXe_TPNPxZ_n@shell.ilvokhin.com/

Signed-off-by: Dmitry Ilvokhin <d@ilvokhin.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Acked-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Link: https://patch.msgid.link/0d998e22a0c595f670cfc6725bb683323aced5cb.1785778551.git.d@ilvokhin.com
---
 include/asm-generic/qspinlock.h | 21 +++++++++++++++++++++
 kernel/Kconfig.locks            | 20 ++++++++++++++++++++
 kernel/locking/qspinlock.c      | 22 ++++++++++++++++++++++
 3 files changed, 63 insertions(+)

diff --git a/include/asm-generic/qspinlock.h b/include/asm-generic/qspinlock.h
index ae45289..2ca94e4 100644
--- a/include/asm-generic/qspinlock.h
+++ b/include/asm-generic/qspinlock.h
@@ -41,6 +41,7 @@
 
 #include <asm-generic/qspinlock_types.h>
 #include <linux/atomic.h>
+#include <linux/tracepoint-defs.h>
 
 #ifndef queued_spin_is_locked
 /**
@@ -130,12 +131,32 @@ static __always_inline void queued_spin_release(struct qspinlock *lock)
 #endif
 
 #ifndef queued_spin_unlock
+
+DECLARE_TRACEPOINT(contended_release);
+
+extern void queued_spin_release_traced(struct qspinlock *lock);
+
 /**
  * queued_spin_unlock - unlock a queued spinlock
  * @lock : Pointer to queued spinlock structure
+ *
+ * Generic tracing wrapper around the arch-overridable
+ * queued_spin_release().
  */
 static __always_inline void queued_spin_unlock(struct qspinlock *lock)
 {
+	/*
+	 * Trace and release are combined in queued_spin_release_traced() so
+	 * the compiler does not need to preserve the lock pointer across the
+	 * function call, avoiding callee-saved register save/restore on the
+	 * hot path. queued_spin_release() is therefore called both here and in
+	 * queued_spin_release_traced(). Keep the two in sync.
+	 */
+	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_QUEUED_SPINLOCKS_TRACE_CONTENDED_RELEASE) &&
+	    tracepoint_enabled(contended_release)) {
+		queued_spin_release_traced(lock);
+		return;
+	}
 	queued_spin_release(lock);
 }
 #endif
diff --git a/kernel/Kconfig.locks b/kernel/Kconfig.locks
index 4198f02..1c6423a 100644
--- a/kernel/Kconfig.locks
+++ b/kernel/Kconfig.locks
@@ -243,6 +243,26 @@ config QUEUED_SPINLOCKS
 	def_bool y if ARCH_USE_QUEUED_SPINLOCKS
 	depends on SMP
 
+config QUEUED_SPINLOCKS_TRACE_CONTENDED_RELEASE
+	bool "Trace contended_release on queued spinlocks"
+	depends on QUEUED_SPINLOCKS && TRACEPOINTS
+	help
+	  Fire the lock:contended_release tracepoint when a contended queued
+	  spinlock is released, so it is possible to attribute a contended
+	  spinlock to its holder.
+
+	  Architectures that can patch the unlock site do this at no cost and
+	  do not need this option.
+
+	  Everywhere else the check is compiled into queued_spin_unlock() and
+	  a small cost is paid on every unlock even when the tracepoint is
+	  disabled: a static-branch NOP and possibly a few more instructions
+	  to manage a stack frame.
+
+	  Sleeping locks fire lock:contended_release regardless of this option.
+
+	  If unsure, say N.
+
 config BPF_ARCH_SPINLOCK
 	bool
 
diff --git a/kernel/locking/qspinlock.c b/kernel/locking/qspinlock.c
index af8d122..33fe6d4 100644
--- a/kernel/locking/qspinlock.c
+++ b/kernel/locking/qspinlock.c
@@ -104,6 +104,28 @@ static __always_inline u32  __pv_wait_head_or_lock(struct qspinlock *lock,
 #define queued_spin_lock_slowpath	native_queued_spin_lock_slowpath
 #endif
 
+#if !defined(queued_spin_unlock) && \
+	IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_QUEUED_SPINLOCKS_TRACE_CONTENDED_RELEASE)
+/*
+ * Out-of-line trace-and-release path for queued_spin_unlock(), used when
+ * the contended_release tracepoint is enabled.
+ *
+ * queued_spin_release() is duplicated here on purpose: doing the release
+ * in this function (rather than tracing here and releasing in the caller)
+ * lets queued_spin_unlock() return right after the call, so the
+ * tracepoint-disabled hot path never has to keep lock live across a call
+ * in a callee-saved register. Keep this release in sync with the one in
+ * queued_spin_unlock().
+ */
+void __lockfunc queued_spin_release_traced(struct qspinlock *lock)
+{
+	if (queued_spin_is_contended(lock))
+		trace_call__contended_release(lock);
+	queued_spin_release(lock);
+}
+EXPORT_SYMBOL(queued_spin_release_traced);
+#endif
+
 #endif /* _GEN_PV_LOCK_SLOWPATH */
 
 /**

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 01/14] mm/memcontrol: Introduce cgroup.memory=tiered_limits boot parameter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new boot parameter 'cgroup.memory=tiered_limits' that enables tier-proportional scaling and enforcement of memory cgroup controller limits. The feature is incompatible with cgroup v1 and raises a warning if a system booted with tiered limits mounts a legacy cgroup. A static key is used to minimize overhead for cgroups not using tier-aware-memcg limits, which will become a hotpath in later commits. The patch adds code to enable the feature at boot time only, as flipping the bit at runtime could lead to uncharged or unchargeable folios.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 02/14] mm/memcontrol: Refactor page_counter charging in try_charge_memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the page_counter charging logic in try_charge_memcg to make it easier to distinguish between memcg v1 and v2 cases, in preparation for adding support for a new page_counter toptier. The changes do not introduce any functional differences, but rather simplify the code structure. This is a precursor to further modifications that will enable charging and uncharging of the new page_counter toptier.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 03/14] mm/memory-tiers: Introduce a mapping from nid to tier_slot
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new data structure called 'tier_slot' which is a dense index that maps node IDs (nid) to tiers, allowing for efficient and fixed mapping of nodes to tiers even when tiers come online or offline at runtime. The patch also adds helper functions to retrieve the nodemask associated with a tier slot. This change enables proper accounting of memory in each tier starting from boot time, addressing issues related to DAX memory hotplugging/hot-unplugging.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 04/14] mm/memcontrol: Allocate per-tier page_counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for tier-aware limits in the Linux memory controller by allocating a page_counter array per memory tier for each mem_cgroup. The array is sized to the number of node IDs and allocated only when tiered limits are enabled, reducing memory usage when the feature is off. The patch also initializes and parent-links every slot in the array during mem_cgroup allocation and frees it during mem_cgroup deallocation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 05/14] mm/memcontrol: Set tier limits proportional to memory limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces proportional tier limits based on memory limits when users write to memory limit sysfs files or when memory hotplug causes tier proportions to shift. The system must have tiered memcg limits enabled for this patch to take effect. It modifies the Linux kernel's memory control and memory tiers code, adding new functions and modifying existing ones to implement proportional tier limits. This change aims to improve the management of memory resources in a multi-tenant environment.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 06/14] mm/vmscan, memcontrol: Add nodemask to try_to_free_mem_cgroup_pages
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new nodemask parameter to the try_to_free_mem_cgroup_pages function in the Linux kernel's memory management subsystem. This allows selective reclaim on specific nodes, enabling future patches to target top-tier nodes and apply downward pressure when their limits are breached but global memcg-wide limits have not yet been reached. The patch modifies several files, including mm/internal.h, mm/memcontrol-v1.c, mm/memcontrol.c, and mm/vmscan.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 07/14] mm/memcontrol: Charge/uncharge tiered memory to mem_cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces tiered memory accounting to the Linux kernel's memory control group (memcg) system. It allows tracking of memory usage on a per-tier basis, where each tier represents a different type of memory. The patch adds functions to charge and uncharge memory for each tier, and updates existing code to use these new functions. This is a necessary step towards enforcing tiered limits on memory usage, which will be implemented in future patches. Currently, this only accounts for LRU folios (memory pages) and does not yet enforce tiered limits.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 08/14] mm/memcontrol: Make memory.low and memory.min tier-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch extends the existing memory.low and memory.min protection to be tier-aware, allowing for proportional best-effort and guaranteed memory protection of higher-tier memory in systems with multiple workloads isolated via the memory cgroup controller. This addresses a limitation where only total memory footprint was enforceable, not where that memory resides. The patch makes no changes unless tiered memcg limits are enabled. It modifies the include/linux/memcontrol.h and mm/memcontrol.c files to implement this new functionality.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 09/14] mm/memcontrol: Make memory.high tier-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch makes the memory.high protection tier-aware, allowing it to enforce a fair distribution of tiered memory among workloads in isolated memory cgroups. It extends the existing memory.high protection by selectively reclaiming on tiers based on limit breaches. When memory.high is breached, it performs reclaim on all tiers. When individual tier limits are breached but memory.high is safe, it performs targeted reclaim on those tiers only. The patch only takes effect when tiered memcg limits are enabled.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 10/14] mm/memcontrol: Make memory.max tier-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch makes the memory.max limit in Linux's memory cgroup controller tier-aware, allowing it to enforce fair distribution of memory among workloads isolated by the controller. The existing limit is extended to consider the page counter of the tier where a folio was allocated, and reclaim is targeted at that tier's nodes when its counter exceeds the limit. This patch also updates the mem_cgroup_margin function to take into account the tier slot, ensuring that the retry check and OOM re-check under oom_lock consider the tier that actually failed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 11/14] mm/memcontrol, migrate: Transfer tier charge on migration
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem in the Linux kernel's memory control system where migrations across different tiers of memory allocation (per-memcg tier limits) can cause the destination tier to exceed its limit. To fix this, the patch introduces a new function `mem_cgroup_migrate_charge` that charges the destination tier separately during migration, attempting to reclaim memory if necessary and failing the migration if not enough headroom is created. The patch also updates existing functions to handle cross-tier migrations correctly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 12/14] mm/memcontrol: Kick async reclaim on migration and folio replacement
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a mechanism to kick asynchronous reclaimers when memory is being migrated or replaced, specifically in cases where soft limits are set and the system has tiered memcg limits enabled. The goal is to prevent forced charges from exceeding high memcg tier limits by triggering async reclaim. The patch adds two new functions: `tier_kick_high` which schedules a work item if the current usage exceeds the high limit, and modifies existing code in `mem_cgroup_replace_folio` and `mem_cgroup_migrate` to call this function when necessary. This approach aims to balance memory usage with soft limits without relying on synchronous reclaim.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 13/14] mm/memcontrol, sched/numa: Gate NUMA promotions into memcg tiers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new condition to gate NUMA promotions into memcg tiers, preventing unnecessary throttling of memory allocations when the destination node has sufficient headroom and the memcg tier is not at its limit. The change adds an additional check in the should_numa_migrate_memory function to consider memcg tier fullness before allowing un-ratelimited promotions. This patch only takes effect on systems with tiered memcg limits enabled, making it a targeted solution for specific use cases.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 14/14] mm/page_alloc: steer allocations away from exhausted memory tiers

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 01/17] selftests/mm: skip collapse_compound_extreme where the PMD is too large
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies a selftest to skip a test case where the PMD (Page Map Directory) size is too large, specifically larger than 32M. The test in question, collapse_compound_extreme, relies on being able to allocate multiple PMD-order allocations, which becomes unreliable for very large PMDs. By skipping this test case when the PMD size exceeds 32M, the patch prevents a failure that would cause the entire binary to stop running and lose subsequent test cases.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 02/17] selftests/mm: scale khugepaged's collapse wait with the PMD size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adjusts the wait time for khugepaged's collapse operation to scale with the PMD size. The original three-second wait is kept as a floor, and an additional second is added per 128M of memory being collapsed. This change aims to prevent false timeouts in cases where the collapse takes longer due to larger PMDs, while still allowing real failures to be reported within a reasonable time frame.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 03/17] selftests/mm: skip khugepaged page cache cases without a PMD folio
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged test suite to skip certain cases related to khugepaged page cache when a PMD folio is not supported. The issue arises from a global cap on page cache order, which prevents PMD-sized page cache folios and causes the kernel to refuse collapses in these cases. The patch adds checks for this condition and skips shmem and file operations if a PMD-order page cache folio is not supported. If no operations are left to collapse into, the test suite exits with a skip message.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 04/17] selftests/mm: retry the swapout the khugepaged swap cases rely on
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged selftest to retry swapout operations when they fail due to a best-effort MADV_PAGEOUT call. The test will wait up to two seconds before reporting failure, allowing for occasional failures caused by folios still under writeback from an earlier pageout. This change is intended to improve the reliability of the khugepaged selftest on certain architectures, such as arm64 with 64K pages.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 05/17] selftests/mm: move is_backed_by_folio() into vm_util
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the is_backed_by_folio() function from split_huge_page_test.c to vm_util.c, making it available for use in other tests. The function checks if an address range is backed by a folio of a given order by reading the compound head and tail flags from /proc/kpageflags. This change allows for more reuse of code across different selftests and does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 06/17] selftests/mm: add folio-order check for address ranges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called `is_range_backed_by_folio_orders` to the Linux kernel's selftests/mm module. The function checks whether an address range is backed by folios of a specific order, and returns true if it is. This is useful for testing memory allocation and deallocation scenarios where folio ordering matters. The function works by checking each window of the address range to see if it maps exactly one folio of the specified order, with the first PFN being the folio head and the subsequent PFNs being contiguous. If any window fails this check, the function returns false.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 07/17] selftests/mm: add folio-order detection self-check
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a self-test to verify that the vm_util folio-order detection helpers agree with the kernel about what backs a mapping. The test faults in memory with only one order enabled and checks that the helpers report exactly that order, not a neighbouring order or plain 4K memory as order 0. This ensures that the helpers are reliable before they are used by khugepaged mTHP tests to detect collapse results.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 08/17] selftests/mm: add khugepaged completion barrier helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a helper function to the selftests/mm module that allows tests to drive the khugepaged daemon in a controlled manner. The helper, called thp_update_num(), writes sysfs knobs only when their values change, preventing unnecessary wake-ups of the daemon. This is necessary because settings pushes must not start scan passes without explicit permission from the caller. The patch also introduces a new function, khugepaged_full_pass(), which drives the daemon in step and waits for full scans to advance by two. This allows tests to check the result of a full scan pass.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 09/17] selftests/mm: add order-parameterized khugepaged collapse cases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds four new test cases to the selftests/mm/khugepaged context, which checks how large pages are collapsed by the khugepaged mechanism. The new cases check each aligned window individually and verify that only the populated window collapses in certain scenarios. Each case faults its region before MADV_HUGEPAGE with only the target order enabled, so the sources are always order 0 and the collapse product can only come from khugepaged. This patch aims to improve the testing of khugepaged's behavior by adding more specific and detailed test cases.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 10/17] selftests/mm: parameterize the mixed-source collapse case by source order
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c test to parameterize the mixed-source collapse case by source order. The test faults a region as order-2 folios and collapses them to the target, but allows for other supported mTHP orders below the target when specified with the -s option. This change is intended to make the test more flexible and adaptable to different system configurations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 11/17] selftests/mm: cover a shared-source collapse write race
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test case to the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c file, which checks for a shared-source collapse write race in the Linux kernel. The test case simulates a scenario where a parent process writes to a shared range while a child process collapses it, and verifies that the content remains isolated during this process. The patch passes on an unmodified kernel, indicating that the isolation provided by khugepaged collapse is sufficient to prevent data corruption. The new test case is designed to ensure that CoW (Copy-on-Write) functionality works correctly in this scenario.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 12/17] selftests/mm: run every supported collapse order by default
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged test to run every supported collapse order by default, rather than requiring the user to specify a specific order. The test will automatically include all anon THP orders below the PMD context in both the no-argument invocation and the 'all' case. This change also updates the handling of the '-c' option, which now pins one order and reports an error if the specified order is above the PMD or unsupported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 13/17] selftests/mm: verify synchronous khugepaged driving is attributable
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test to verify that synchronous khugepaged driving is attributable and deterministic. The test uses the huge_memory tracepoints to attribute outcomes and checks that exactly one collapse attempt is made on each prepared window, resulting in the window being collapsed afterwards. The test also sets scan_sleep_millisecs to 60s to prove the wake path. The patch adds a new selftest called khugepaged_sync_check and modifies several files to support it.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 14/17] selftests/mm: add khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a selftest harness to exercise the khugepaged functionality under concurrent access scenarios, including faults, GUP pins, fork, mremap, and MADV_DONTNEED operations. The test simulates three different driver modes: stepped (khugepaged running one full pass at a time), free (khugepaged left to run without any intervention), and madvise (MADV_COLLAPSE and MADV_DONTNEED loop). The test ensures that the racing pages are either read as their pattern or as zero, never anything else. The kernel's own assertions are also used to verify the correctness of the test.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 15/17] selftests/mm: race collapse of windows with holes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged_race test to run both ends of the occupancy scale, one after the other, for every driver mode. The test checks for correctness by verifying that every racing page reads as its pattern or zero. The patch also adds a new option -z to narrow a run to the hole-heavy end, and another option -m to narrow it to one mode. This is done to collapse windows with holes, which was not happening before due to the harness pinning max_ptes_none to 0.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 16/17] selftests/mm: add memory-pressure threads to the khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new threads to the khugepaged race harness, which tests the Linux kernel's memory management under various stress conditions. The first thread, 'pageout', simulates swap traffic and LRU churn by repeatedly MADV_PAGEOUTing a dedicated region of memory and checking its contents after each cycle. The second thread, 'compactor', triggers compaction by writing to /proc/sys/vm/compact_memory in a loop, competing with the collapse for pages and refcount elevations. The patch also introduces new command-line options to narrow down the test runs to specific combinations of modes and occupancy limits.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 17/17] selftests/mm: zap whole PTE tables in the khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged race harness to occasionally zap a whole PMD-aligned area of pages, rather than just individual pages or tables. This is done to test the empty-table reclaim functionality, which only engages when a zap spans an entire table. The change introduces occasional whole-table zaps every 64 iterations, while maintaining the existing fine-grained page zapping as the common case.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch series improves the coverage of khugepaged selftests by adding new cases and reworking existing ones to better test the collapse mechanism. It includes tests for folio-order detection, order-parameterized collapse cases, and shared-source write races. The patches also scale the collapse wait time with PMD size and fix issues in existing cases.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 02/11] mm, swap: support zswap and zeroswap as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces support for virtual swap (vswap) in the Linux kernel, allowing pages to be compressed by zswap or detected as zero-filled without pre-allocating a physical swap slot. It builds on top of the existing swap-table infrastructure and supports zswap and zero-page backends. The vswap layer decouples PTE swap entries from physical backing, enabling efficient compression and detection of zero-filled pages. The patch also adds a sysctl to enable or disable vswap allocation at runtime and introduces a new build option for defaulting vswap on or off. However, it does not yet support physical disk backing or real writeback, which will be addressed in subsequent patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 03/11] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the Linux kernel's swap IO path to support virtual swap (vswap) by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. The sector is computed from an explicit entry and passed through various functions, enabling batching of both vswap entries and physical entries mapped directly into PTEs. Although there are no functional changes yet, this patch sets the stage for adding a physical swap backend for vswap.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 04/11] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer (vswap). When zswap declines a page, it allocates a physical slot on demand for swap out. The patch tracks each vswap entry's physical slot via a pointer-tagged swap_table entry and modifies readahead to skip these entries. It also adds writeback of zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap and reclaim of physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries, which are handled in subsequent patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 05/11] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables THP (Transparent Huge Pages) swapin for vswap entries by checking the backing's THP amenability under a cluster lock in __swap_cache_add_check. It rejects ZSWAP and mixed batches via -EBUSY, triggering order-fallback. The patch also updates various files to handle this new behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 06/11] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap, mirroring the existing zswap writeback path but allocating a physical slot on demand at writeback time rather than pre-allocating it. It also relaxes the zswap shrinker gate by replacing a blanket check with can_zswap_writeback(), which only skips when no physical slot is free to allocate. This allows the shrinker to drain vswap entries when physical swap is available.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 07/11] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch reclaims physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries to free up physical capacity for new allocations when the swap space is more than half used. A vswap entry becomes cache-only when its swap_count drops to zero but the folio remains in the swap cache, making the associated physical slot redundant and reclaimable. The patch introduces a flag to mark such slots as cache-only and adds code to reclaim them from the physical reclaim scanner.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 08/11] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory management to only charge physical swap entries when they acquire actual backing, rather than immediately upon allocation. This change ensures that memory.swap.current accurately reflects on-disk swap usage and prevents zswap-backed pages from being counted as occupying swap space. As a result, cgroups with all pages in zswap can now reclaim anonymous memory even if memory.swap.max is set to 0.

memory.swap.* are about physical swap space. They track, control, and

inside the zeromap without consuming swapfile space, these counters
must be 0.

When a user switches on vswap to use zswap without a backing file,
these counters must be 0.

When a user switches on vswap to use zswap with writeback, only the
pages that get written to the swapfile must be tracked and controlled
by these counters.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 09/11] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track the usage of virtual swap slots in Linux. The 'used' counter tracks the number of pages currently allocated, while the 'alloc_reject' counter tracks the cumulative number of pages that failed to get a vswap slot. This allows for better monitoring and debugging of vswap performance issues.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 10/11] mm, swap: defer memcg_table allocation for physical swap clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory allocation in the Linux kernel's swap management by deferring the allocation of a memcg table for physical swap clusters that only hold vswap backings. This is done to reduce unnecessary memory usage and improve performance on workloads where zswap writeback is the primary consumer of physical swap. The patch introduces a new condition to allocate the memcg table eagerly only when it's known to be needed, such as in non-VSWAP builds or for vswap clusters. For physical clusters in VSWAP builds, the allocation is deferred until the first direct-use slot is encountered.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 11/11] mm, swap: widen swap_info_struct max/pages to unsigned long
series_items.patch_summary: This patch widens the max and pages fields in swap_info_struct from unsigned int to unsigned long, allowing the vswap device to exceed its current limit of 16 TB (16 terabytes) and reach a new maximum of approximately 8 petabytes. This change is necessary because the cluster_info_pool xarray's allocator limit exceeds the original limit. The physical swap remains unaffected by this change.

The patch is pure scaffolding and does not yet enable swapon or swapoff operations on the virtual device. It lays the groundwork for subsequent patches to implement the vswap-aware swap-out, swap-in, and writeback paths.

      vswap-backing slot installs. Saves ~512 bytes per physical cluster

    * Widen swap_info_struct->max and ->pages (and the swapoff unuse-path
      index) so vswap supports ~8 PB of swap space (this is the new

    * Split the physical-swap-backend patch into three for reviewability:

      (patch 4), and reclaim of cache-only physical slots (patch 5). No
      functional change.
    * Add kerneldoc for the vswap API.
    * Add some benchmark numbers for zswap case.


I. Context and Motivation
=========================

Currently, when an anon page is swapped out, a slot in a backing swap
device is allocated and stored in the page table entries that refer to
the original page. This slot is also used as the "key" to find the
swapped out content, as well as the index to swap data structures, such
as the swap cache, or the swap cgroup mapping. Tying a swap entry to its
backing slot in this way is performant and efficient when swap is purely
just disk space, and swapoff is rare.

However, the advent of many swap optimizations has exposed major
drawbacks of this design. The first problem is that we occupy a physical
slot in the swap space, even for pages that are NEVER expected to hit
the disk: pages compressed and stored in the zswap pool, zero-filled
pages, or pages rejected by both of these optimizations when zswap
writeback is disabled. This is arguably the central shortcoming of
zswap:
* Resource-wise, it is hugely wasteful in terms of disk usage. At Meta,
  we size swapfile in the order of 25-50% of host RAM, depending on flash
  availaiblity. This is a lot of flash for a fleet of our size, and
  with universal zswap enablement, most of this is wasted for zswap
  entries.

* In deployments when no disk space can be afforded for swap (such as
  mobile and embedded devices), users cannot adopt zswap, and are forced
  to use zram. This is confusing for users, and creates extra burdens
  for developers, having to develop and maintain similar features for
  two separate swap backends (writeback, cgroup charging, THP support,
  etc.). For instance, see the discussion in [2].

* Tying zswap (and more generally, other in-memory swap backends) to
  the current physical swapfile infrastructure makes zswap implicitly
  statically sized. This does not make sense, as unlike disk swap, in
  which we consume a limited resource (disk space or swapfile space) to
  save another resource (memory), zswap consumes the same resource it is
  saving (memory). The more we zswap, the more memory we have available,
  not less. We are not rationing a limited resource when we limit
  the size of the zswap pool, but rather we are capping the resource
  (memory) saving potential of zswap. Under memory pressure, using
  more zswap is almost always better than the alternative (disk IOs, or
  even worse, OOMs), and dynamically sizing the zswap pool on demand
  allows the system to flexibly respond to these precarious scenarios.

* Operationally, static provisioning the swapfile for zswap poses
  significant challenges, because the sysadmin has to prescribe how
  much swap is needed a priori, for each combination of
  (memory size x disk space x workload usage). It is even more
  complicated when we take into account the variance of memory
  compression, which changes the reclaim dynamics (and as a result,
  swap space size requirement). The problem is further exacerbated for
  users who rely on swap utilization (and exhaustion) as an OOM signal.

  All of these factors make it very difficult to configure the swapfile
  for zswap: too small of a swapfile and we risk preventable OOMs and
  limit the memory saving potentials of zswap; too big of a swapfile
  and we waste disk space and memory due to swap metadata overhead.
  This dilemma becomes more drastic in high memory systems, which can
  have up to TBs worth of memory.

Swap virtualization is the answer to these issues, with three properties:

1. Decoupled backends. For zswap in particular, this means we eliminate
   the unused storage space, and allows zswap to be used in systems that
   do not have enough storage capacity for physical swap (without having
   to resort to silly hacks). Zero-filled swap pages and swap-cache-only
   folios also benefit here.

2. Dynamic swap space. Since virtual swap is not tied to any physical
   resource, we can make it infinite and dynamically grow it on demand.
   This massively simplifies operational provisioning, and increases the
   utilization of compressed swap backends (zswap). Dynamicity also
   reduces overhead on unused swap capacity.

3. Efficient backend transfer. The virtualization scheme should not
   introduce PTE/rmap walking overhead for backend transfer. This
   is crucial for systems that want to support multiple swap backends
   in a tiering fashion (for e.g zswap -> disk swap).

For more historical contexts and references, please take a look at
the cover letter of the older vswap submissions ([3] and [v2]).

II. Design
==========

When we compile kernel with CONFIG_VSWAP, a special vswap device is
allocated at boot time, and all swapped out pages try to allocate from
this device first, falling back to a physical swap device on failure.

Routing can also be turned off at runtime with the vm.vswap_enabled
sysctl, which defaults to 0 unless CONFIG_VSWAP_DEFAULT_ON=y. It is
allocation-only: new swapouts go straight to physical swap, while
entries already backed by vswap keep being served and drain as they
are faulted back in or freed.

These swap entries can subsequently acquire backend on-demand, such as
a zswap entry, or a slot on a physical swap device.

We repurpose much of the existing swap_table infrastructure and
swapfile allocator for this new vswap device, with two notable
differences:
* Clusters are dynamically allocated on demand and managed through
  an xarray. This in turn allows us to avoid static provisioning and
  let swap space grow dynamically.

* Each cluster of this new vswap device has a virtual_table that stores
  the backend information of the entries in the cluster (see below).

struct swap_cluster_info_dynamic {
    struct swap_cluster_info ci;       /* swap_table, lock, etc. */
    unsigned int index;                /* position in xarray */
    struct rcu_head rcu;               /* kfree_rcu deferred free */
    atomic_long_t *virtual_table;      /* backend info, 8 B/slot */
};

Each vswap cluster (swap_cluster_info_dynamic) extends the classic
swap_cluster_info struct with a virtual_table array that stores the
backend information for each virtual swap entry in the cluster. Each
entry is tag-encoded in the low 3 bits to indicate the backend type:

  NONE:     |----- 0000 ------|000|  free / unbacked
  SWAPFILE: |- type:5,off:56 -|001|  on a physical swapfile
  ZSWAP:    |--- zswap_entry* |010|  compressed in zswap

Other design highlights:

* Note that for the vswap device, we have merged the zswap xarray tree
  with the swapfile-level clusters. This means that for zswap only users,
  we have negligible extra space overhead.

* Both vswap entries (Case 1) and directly-mapped physical entries
  (Case 2) coexist as first-class citizens. When CONFIG_VSWAP=n the
  vswap paths compile out.

* Backend transitions in the virtual_table are synchronized through the
  swap cache and the folio lock - the same mechanism that already
  serializes ordinary swap operations (swapin, swapout, zswap
  writeback, swap cache reclaim). IOW, we can only assume that the
  backend of a vswap entry is stable through swap cache/folio lock.
  Looking at the backend without this should be done at best for
  optimization purposes, as there is no guarantee that the backend
  will not change under the observer.

* Pointer-tagged swap_table entries on physical clusters provide the
  rmap (physical -> virtual) lookup.

* Virtual swap slots not backed by physical swap are not charged to
  memcg swap counters - only physical backing is charged (I made the
  case for this in [4]).


III. Benchmarks
===============

Note that the goal is not to match vswap performance with baseline on
every single case yet - we still maintain !CONFIG_VSWAP setup. We can
optimize further once we have landed this new feature.

A. Production Workload: Instagram
=================================

To test vswap's stability and performance, I ran an A/B experiment on
Instagram (django) workload, with zswap as the swap backend. On these
hosts, the swapfiles' size is 50% of RAM.

Compared to baseline, vswap gives:

* On par request throughput.
* Lower request serving latency (by about 1-3%).
* Lower memory pressure in the system service cgroups running alongside
  the workload. PSI-based proactive reclaimer can therefore recover more
  from them, lowering their overall memory footprint, allowing the main
  workload to expand.
* Elimination of swapfile footprint for all zswap users in the host.

In the RFC v2 ([v2]), I put out several theories for this. I have
done some prototyping to isolate effects, and it turns out the
performance wins come primarily from the elimination of zswap's
xarray and the merging of zswap's metadata to swap device's cluster.
Several code paths are optimized thanks to this - for instance,
in swap_range_free(), we call zswap_invalidate() once for each entry the
range, resulting in multiple xarray tree walks. With vswap, we perform
one single xarray walk to grab a 512-slot cluster, then performs a
flat array scan to free zswap metadata. Similar wins can be observed
in Baoquan's optimization ([8]), which also optimizes away the zswap tree.

Appendix: Alternative Designs and Improvements
==============================================

A. Vmalloc Data Structure:
==========================

This is a promising alternative to the xarray data structure, reducing
the indirection overhead. The initial version relies on userspace knob to
trigger swap address space growth - I have commented on why this is shaky
in [5].

Baoquan has followed-up with a new version (see [6]) that should give us
kernel-driven dynamic growth and (tail-only) shrink. This seems sufficient
for vswap use case, AFAICT - but seems like it would need a couple more
versions to finalize the design.

I think it is better to proceed with the xarray data structure first,
especially since we already see some positive signals on performance
by storing zswap metadata in a per-cluster flat table. With vswap landed,
we will have a concrete setup to show vmalloc data structure's wins.

B. Moving the backend table to struct swap_cluster_info
=======================================================

Another approach Baoquan and I discussed on is to structure vswap patch
series as follows:

1. Moving vtable (renamed to something more generic) to swap cluster,
   which removes the xarray.

2. Once vswap is introduced, we simply use this field to store the
   backend.

I have a prototype for this, but I ended up scrapping the whole thing, for
the following reasons:

1. It ended up being even more code than what I sent out here - most of
   which touches the non-vswap code paths, which we either want to leave
   alone (generic swap logic) or want to rip out wholesale down the line
   (zswap).

2. There are several fields that are ONLY needed for the vswap clusters
   (for instance, rcu_head and index). Shoving them into the shared struct
   swap_cluster_info imposes memory and mental overhead for non-vswap
   clusters and users.

   We can avoid this by simply moving it to the wrapper struct
   (swap_cluster_info_dynamic). This is actually Kairui's design
   (see [7]), but after trying to deviate from it, I have to conclude
   it is the right choice too.

3. Replacing zswap tree with the per-cluster backend table results in
   performance wins even when vswap is turned off (this is how I
   verified that vswap's performance wins comes from here).

   However, it requires more code to make sure this table is not allocated
   when not needed. Note that the eventual goal is to make vswap the ONLY
   way to use zswap, so we are literally adding complexity and overhead
   (even for non-vswap users) to optimize for a code path that is rarely
   exercised after vswap lands, and will be ripped out soon after.
   That seems very off to me.

To close out, this design brings together the ideas from the earlier
discussions:

1. All of the requirements I set out to solve (dynamicity, backend
   decoupling, efficient backend transfer) are implemented.

2. Vswap device now repurpose the swap table design and most of the
   generic swap operations.

3. Minimal overhead for non-vswap users, and zswap-no-writeback users.
   If you disable writeback, vswap *is* a ghost swapfile.

To head off any uncertainty about this: this is exactly what needs to
happen in terms of cgroup semantics.

memory.swap.* are about physical swap space. They track, control, and
enforce fairness for a finite resource that is separate from memory.

When a user switches on vswsap and a bunch of empty pages are stored
inside the zeromap without consuming swapfile space, these counters
must be 0.

When a user switches on vswap to use zswap without a backing file,
these counters must be 0.

When a user switches on vswap to use zswap with writeback, only the
pages that get written to the swapfile must be tracked and controlled
by these counters.
